children: By Julie Jargon
After a wild week of bank, email and travel outages, we now have something else to worry about: scams seizing on the chaos.

The Microsoft server upgrade that resulted in a 19-hour email interruption was quickly followed by what Microsoft described as a global "high-volume phishing campaign." Scammers sent fake emails about disconnected accounts and other troubles to get people to click on malicious links.
Cybersecurity experts warn that disruptions like the recent FAA ground stop, United Airlines' communications outage and Chase's transaction delays can also open the door to opportunistic fraudsters.

Scammers aren't always reaching out to consumers directly when crises unfold — sometimes all they have to do is wait for potential victims to come to them. Bad actors know people will google their airline or bank to find a phone number when there is a problem, so they create fake customer-service websites that appear high in internet search results.

"Sometimes you create the urgency yourself, because you hear about something on the news and fear your money is at risk," says Iskander Sanchez-Rola, senior director of AI and innovation for digital security brand Norton. "You find a fake number and call them."
It happened to me.
I bought concert tickets then noticed the date wasn't right. I googled Ticketmaster and called the number that came up in the AI overview to inquire about it.

The man who answered acted as though he knew all about it. He said that to get a refund, I had to verify my identity by purchasing an Apple gift card and read him the code. I hung up and went to Ticketmaster's website, which showed an entirely different phone number.
As we head into the biggest travel and shopping season of the year, it is a good time to be aware of what to do — and what not to do — to protect yourself from scams.
Travel

A common tactic during travel disruptions, according to cybersecurity company McAfee, is for scammers to send messages about a flight change or cancellation. They give a deadline to rebook, such as 30 minutes, to induce panic. The link they provide directs the would-be victim to a fraudulent website or call center where operators ask for credit-card information, airline login credentials or other personal information.
Don't call a number or click a link sent to you in an alleged cancellation text or email.

Instead, go to your airline's website or app, verify your flight's actual status, and call the customer-service number listed. Take a close look at the web address to make sure you aren't visiting a spoofed site. At the airport already? Check the departure board or speak with an agent.
Banking

Scammers sometimes impersonate bank representatives. (They play the odds, since so many Americans use Chase, Bank of America and Wells Fargo.) They tell people their account is compromised or locked and they must log in or transfer money to protect the funds.

If you receive a text, email or phone call from what appears to be your bank, informing you of a data breach or service disruption, verify it. Check the phone number printed on your bank card, bank statement or in your bank's app or website, Sanchez-Rola says.
Never transfer or withdraw funds or buy cryptocurrency at the urging of someone who calls you claiming to represent your bank.
Email

Following the Microsoft 365 outage, users received emails that appeared to come from the company. Some said stalled messages would be deleted in 24 hours unless users took action. Microsoft said the goal was likely to capture login credentials.

"Cybercriminals love a crisis, and outages or other moments of uncertainty can give them an opening. We've seen phishing campaigns exploit recent service disruptions, using familiar branding and urgent warnings," Tanmay Ganacharya, corporate vice president of Microsoft Security, said in a statement. "Microsoft continues to monitor for these threats and block malicious domains and phishing messages."

If you receive any kind of email from a service provider or other important institution, check the sender's address. If it isn't exactly right — a spelling error, extra text on the end — it is probably fraudulent. Still unclear? Log in to your account or call the appropriate customer-service line to see if the issue is real.
"Most of the time you shouldn't do anything," Sanchez-Rola says. "It's very unlikely a company will reach out directly to individuals to solve a problem they have, such as an outage."
More best practices

Slow down. "Urgency is the biggest thing scammers use to get you," says Perry Olsen, a Salt Lake City-based cybersecurity expert who shares digital safety tips on Instagram. He advises taking a deep breath and going straight to the source.

Enable two-factor authentication. Any online account you depend on should require at least two steps to log in, which can mean generating a code or receiving it on another device or account. Here are tips for activating it.

Manage your passwords. They should be strong and unique for each account. Password managers can help organize all of that. They also protect you by not filling in your login information on spoof sites created by hackers. If you ever type your credentials on any site you later believe was fraudulent, change your password ASAP.

Avoid googling. Save airline, bank and other important phone numbers in your contacts. Get that information from your cards, apps or trusted websites, not by searching online. Bookmark those important websites so you don't accidentally open the wrong one in a crisis.

Don't pay anyone anything. If a company randomly reaches out to urgently request you to transfer funds, either by Venmo or Zelle or via gift cards, you have to stop and think to yourself: Why on earth would they do that?
